title: Batch ingestion patterns
summary: How to pull data from databases, files and APIs on a schedule without losing rows, duplicating rows or overloading the source.

blocks.text: Most data still arrives in batches: a job wakes up, asks a source what changed, and lands the result in bronze (chapter 13). Batch ingestion looks simple, which is why it fails quietly. The property that makes all of it recoverable is the idempotent load.
16.1 Full versus incremental extracts

A **full extract** reads the whole table each run and replaces the target copy. It is correct by construction: deletes and late updates cannot hide. Its cost grows with table size. An **incremental extract** reads only rows changed since the last run and merges them; its cost grows with change volume, but it needs a trustworthy change column.

head: Aspect
Full
Incremental
rows: No, unless soft deletes or CDC

blocks.text: A table that fully extracts in a minute or two is usually cheaper to reload than to maintain incremental logic for. Many teams combine both: incremental hourly, plus a weekly full reconciliation that catches what the incremental path missed.
Keep full snapshots in bronze as dated partitions. Diffing two snapshots is a cheap way to derive deletes and build SCD type 2 history (chapter 9) for sources that offer nothing better.
16.2 High-watermark columns and their traps
An incremental extract stores a **high watermark**: the highest value of a change column (`updated_at`, a sequence, a row version) seen by the last successful run.

blocks.title: Postgres: bounded window with overlap
blocks.text:
-- :low  = stored watermark minus a lookback (e.g. 15 minutes)
-- :high = timestamp captured at job start
SELECT id, customer_id, status, total_amount, updated_at
FROM shop.orders
WHERE updated_at >  :low
  AND updated_at <= :high;
The **upper bound** makes the window unambiguous; `:high` becomes the next watermark, written only after the target load commits.

items: **Late commits.** `updated_at` is set when the statement runs, not when the transaction commits. A long transaction can commit rows stamped before the last watermark; they are never re-read. Fix: a lookback overlap plus an idempotent merge.
**Clock skew.** Values set by application hosts disagree by seconds. Prefer database-assigned values.
**Unmaintained columns.** Admin scripts and bulk fixes often skip `updated_at`. Profile before trusting it.
**Hard deletes** leave nothing to select. Use soft-delete flags, key-only full extracts to anti-join, or CDC (chapter 17).
**Insert-only ids.** An auto-increment id catches inserts, never updates.

blocks.text: Deriving the next watermark as `max(updated_at)` from the target breaks when a single future-dated row arrives: every later run skips everything older. Store the run's own `:high` and alert on future timestamps.
16.3 ELT tools: Fivetran, Airbyte, dlt
Writing extractors for many SaaS APIs and databases is undifferentiated work, so most teams adopt connectors.

head: Tool
Model
Notable mechanics
rows: Managed SaaS, priced on monthly active rows
Maintained connectors, log-based CDC for many databases, metadata columns such as `_fivetran_synced` and `_fivetran_deleted`
Connector catalogue and builder; sync modes such as full refresh and incremental append or append-deduped
Schema inference and evolution, incremental cursors, append / replace / merge dispositions

blocks.text: Underneath, all of them do the same things: a cursor or log position per stream, state persisted between runs, metadata columns for load time and deletion, and a merge on a key. Knowing that lets you debug them.

blocks.title: dlt: incremental merge resource
blocks.text:
import dlt

@dlt.resource(primary_key='id', write_disposition='merge')
def orders(updated_at=dlt.sources.incremental('updated_at', initial_value='2024-01-01T00:00:00Z')):
    # fetch_orders is your own paginated API client
    yield from fetch_orders(updated_since=updated_at.last_value)

pipeline = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name='shop', destination='snowflake', dataset_name='raw_shop')
pipeline.run(orders())
16.4 File drops and APIs

blocks.title: A robust file-drop pipeline
blocks.caption: The load log keyed by path and content hash makes reruns and resends safe.

items: **Partial files**: agree on a completion marker or atomic rename so readers never load half an upload.
**Resends**: decide whether a corrected file replaces the earlier load (delete by file name, reload) or is rejected.
**Bookkeeping**: Snowflake `COPY INTO` skips files it already loaded into the table (its load metadata expires after 64 days); beyond that you need your own log.
**Lineage**: land the file name (`METADATA$FILENAME` in Snowflake, `_metadata.file_path` in Spark) so a bad file can be removed.

blocks.text: SaaS APIs paginate and throttle. **Offset pagination** shifts when rows change during a crawl, causing gaps and duplicates; **cursor** or **keyset** pagination (`updated_after` plus `after_id`) is stable. Honour `429` responses and `Retry-After` with exponential backoff and jitter, checkpoint the cursor so a crash does not restart at page one, and land raw JSON before flattening so you can re-parse history without calling the API again.
Many APIs never expose hard deletes and limit how far back incremental queries can look. Check the API documentation before promising complete history.
16.5 Idempotent loads and backfills

A load is **idempotent** when running it twice for the same input leaves the target as running it once. Retries, overlaps and backfills then become safe. Three shapes: **partition overwrite** (each run owns and replaces a partition), **delete-insert** by batch key in one transaction, and **MERGE** on a business key keeping the newest version.

blocks.title: Snowflake: idempotent merge of an overlapping batch
blocks.text:
MERGE INTO silver.orders AS t
USING (
    SELECT * FROM bronze.orders_batch
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
) AS s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET
    status = s.status, total_amount = s.total_amount, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, customer_id, status, total_amount, updated_at)
    VALUES (s.id, s.customer_id, s.status, s.total_amount, s.updated_at);
`QUALIFY` removes duplicate versions (several source rows matching one target row is an error or non-deterministic), and the timestamp guard stops a replayed old row overwriting newer data.

For **backfills**, parameterise every job by window (`start`, `end`) rather than `now()`, so a backfill is just many runs over old windows, chunked and throttled against the source. Airflow data intervals and Dagster partitions model this directly (chapter 30).

blocks.title: Use case: the missing invoice lines
blocks.text: A retailer extracts ERP invoice lines nightly with `updated_at > last_max`. Finance totals are slightly below the ERP. Long posting batches commit after midnight with rows stamped before midnight.
items: Bounded windows with a two-hour lookback and a MERGE on line id.
A weekly key-and-amount reconciliation against the source, kept as a quality check (chapter 33).

blocks.text: 16.6 Protecting the source

Extraction queries hit systems that serve customers. Read from a replica, index the watermark column, chunk by key range and agree extraction windows with the owning team. When freshness needs outgrow polling, log-based CDC (chapter 17) removes most of the query load.

blocks.title: Plan three ingestions
blocks.text: Ingest (a) a 40 million row Postgres `orders` table with reliable `updated_at` but hard deletes, (b) a CRM API with cursor pagination and a low rate limit, and (c) daily partner CSVs that are sometimes resent corrected. For each, choose full or incremental, the state you store, how deletes are handled and how a rerun stays idempotent.
hints: Which source can tell you about deletes at all?
What do a resent file and its original share?
Where does the API cursor live if the worker crashes?

items: Full extracts catch deletes; incremental extracts scale with change volume but need a reliable change column.
Bound windows, overlap with a lookback, absorb duplicates with an idempotent MERGE.
Watermarks miss late commits, skewed clocks, untouched columns and hard deletes.
ELT tools implement cursors, state, metadata columns and merges.
Files need completion markers and a load log; APIs need checkpointed pagination and backoff.
Window-parameterised jobs make backfills ordinary reruns.

blocks.q: An incremental job filters `updated_at > last_watermark` with no lookback. What is it most exposed to?
options: Losing rows from transactions that commit late with an earlier `updated_at`
blocks.explain: `updated_at` reflects statement time, not commit time, so late commits fall behind the watermark. Duplicates appear only once you add overlap, which is why overlap is paired with an idempotent merge.

blocks.q: Why deduplicate the MERGE source with `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER()`?
options: Several source rows matching one target row cause an error or an arbitrary result
blocks.explain: Overlapping windows produce multiple versions per key; you must pick the latest explicitly. MERGE does not silently ignore duplicate matches.

blocks.q: Which approach detects hard deletes when the source only has `updated_at`?
options: Periodic key-only extracts anti-joined with the target
blocks.explain: A deleted row changes no timestamp, so frequency and operators do not help. Comparing key sets (or CDC) reveals vanished keys; `>=` only fixes boundary ties.

blocks.q: What makes backfilling last month safe while the daily schedule keeps running?
options: Window-parameterised jobs loading into idempotent targets
blocks.explain: With explicit windows and idempotent loads, a backfill is just more runs and overlaps are harmless. Jobs based on `now()` cannot target the past; warehouse size affects speed, not correctness.
